**The Collector**

In the basement of an unremarkable house on the edge of town, Elias kept his gallery. The walls were lined with what looked, at a distance, like lifelike hunting trophies—except these were people. Men and women frozen in poses of quiet dignity or startled surprise, their skin preserved and stretched over carefully sculpted forms, eyes replaced with polished glass orbs that caught the lamplight. He called them his "finest specimens." They had all come to him willingly at first, drawn by charm or desperation, and none had ever left.

Tonight’s addition was a woman named Lena. She had been a hitchhiker, trusting and talkative for the first thirty miles. Now she lay on the long steel table under the harsh fluorescent lights, already drained and cooled.

Elias worked methodically, the way his father had taught him with deer and foxes long ago. First he made the long ventral incision from throat to pelvis, parting the skin with steady strokes of the scalpel. He peeled it back in careful layers, working the blade between dermis and muscle so the hide came away intact. The inner surface was cleaned of clinging tissue with a solution of borax and salt, then set aside to cure while he turned to the body.

He removed the viscera in sections, rinsing the cavity thoroughly. For the limbs and torso he packed the spaces with a dense mixture of sawdust, clay, and expanding foam to restore natural contours. The skull was emptied through the foramen magnum, the brain tissue scooped out and replaced with a lightweight urethane cast. Wires ran through the limbs and spine to hold the posture he had chosen—an upright, slightly turned stance with one hand extended, as though she were offering something unseen.

Once the form was set and the skin completely dry, Elias fitted it back over the mannequin like a tailored garment. He stitched the long seam closed with fine waxed thread, smoothing every wrinkle. Glass eyes—hazel, to match the original—were set into the sockets and secured. A light brushing of preservative powder along the seams, a final combing of the hair, and she was finished.

He wheeled her into the display room on a small platform and positioned her between a stern-looking man in a business suit and a smiling girl in a sundress. Stepping back, Elias studied the arrangement with satisfaction. The three figures looked almost conversational, as if they might resume a discussion at any moment.

“Welcome home,” he said softly, and turned off the lights.

The collection waited in the dark, perfectly still.

The wind howled through the fractured fuselage like something alive and furious, but inside the wreck the only sounds were the wet, labored breathing of the dying and the silence of those who had already stopped. Five days. Five days of nothing but melted snow and the faint sweetness of pine needles they had tried to chew for bulk. The cold had hollowed them out; the hunger had done worse. It had become a separate creature living behind their eyes.

They had drawn lots without saying the word. When the lot fell to Elena, she was the one who took the pocket knife from the dead man’s pack. His name had been Marcus. He had been the strongest of them after the impact, the one who kept insisting help would come. A compound fracture in his femur had turned septic by the third day. By the fifth he was already gone, though his body had not yet understood.

Elena knelt beside him. Her hands shook so violently the blade tapped against her knee. She could smell him—not rot yet, just the iron scent of old blood and the faint, sweet smell of dying tissue. Her stomach clenched and unclawed at the same time, a sickening double motion.

She told herself the sentence she had rehearsed: *He is not here anymore. This is only meat. Meat keeps you alive.* The thought felt like swallowing glass. She pressed the tip of the knife to the inside of his thigh where the muscle was thickest and still relatively untouched by injury. The resistance of skin surprised her; it did not want to yield. When the blade finally parted it, the sound was intimate and wet, like cloth tearing underwater.

Her gorge rose so hard she had to turn her head and spit bile into the snow. For a moment the world narrowed to a single, crystalline point: if she did this, something fundamental would tear inside her the way the skin had torn. There would be no coming back across that line. She could already feel the future version of herself watching, the one who would never again be able to pretend she was only an animal following instinct. This was choice. This was the moment the animal stepped forward and the person who had once argued philosophy over coffee stepped back.

She cut a strip no larger than her finger. It was shockingly red against the snow. Her breath came in short, animal pants. She brought it to her mouth and held it there, the smell metallic and wrong. Every part of her that had ever been human recoiled. The hunger did not recoil. It simply waited, patient and absolute.

When she finally closed her teeth, the texture was nothing like meat she had known. It was dense and gave too easily. The taste flooded her—copper and something darker, almost sweet at the edges. She did not chew so much as survive the act of swallowing. Her mind split cleanly in two: one part catalogued the nutrients, the warmth, the sudden animal gratitude; the other part stood at a distance, watching a woman she used to recognize commit an irrevocable desecration.

She took the second bite because the first had not killed her. By the third she was no longer thinking in sentences. Only later, when the others came closer with their eyes averted and their hands shaking in identical rhythm, did the full weight of what she had broken settle over her like new snow. She had stepped through a door that did not open from the other side. The cold was still there. The hunger was quieter, but it would return. And she would never again be able to pretend she did not know exactly what she was capable of when the cold and the hunger spoke together.

The fluorescent lights buzzed overhead like angry hornets as Marcus jolted awake, his wrists shackled to the cold metal table. A grainy videotape whirred to life on the battered TV in front of him. The puppet’s painted face leered from the screen.

“Hello, Marcus. You’ve spent your life devouring everything in your path without consequence. Now the table is turned. Before you sits your only key to freedom. Consume it—all of it—before the acid in the vents reaches your lungs. You have three minutes.”

The screen went black. A timer on the wall began its merciless countdown: 2:59… 2:58…

On the stainless-steel tray in front of him lay a glistening, gray-pink coil of raw pig intestine, still slick with half-congealed blood and flecked with bits of undigested feed. Live mealworms writhed through the folds like pale, squirming commas. A sour, metallic reek hit him first—ammonia, copper, and the sweet-rot smell of offal left too long in the heat. His stomach lurched before he even touched it.

Marcus’s hands shook as he lifted a section of the intestine. It was warm, rubbery, and yielded under his fingers with a wet, sucking sound. A worm slipped free and landed on his wrist; he felt its tiny legs scrabbling against his skin. Bile rose instantly, burning the back of his throat. He forced his jaws apart and bit down.

The first chew was a nightmare of textures: the intestine split with a soft pop, releasing a hot, ferrous flood across his tongue. The worms crunched between his molars—brittle shells giving way to soft, squirming centers that burst with a faint, grassy bitterness. He gagged hard, shoulders jerking, but the chain kept his head forward. Thick saliva flooded his mouth; he swallowed convulsively, the mass sliding down his throat like a living thing trying to crawl back up.

Tears streamed down his face. Another bite. This time the worm he caught thrashed against the roof of his mouth before he crushed it. The taste turned fecal, metallic, and cloyingly sweet all at once. His esophagus spasmed; he retched, a rope of mucus and half-chewed meat hanging from his lips. He shoved it back in with trembling fingers and kept chewing, eyes squeezed shut, breath coming in wet, panicked hitches.

By the second minute the tray was half-empty and his stomach was in full revolt. Every swallow triggered a fresh heave that left him bent double, forehead pressed to the cold metal while his body tried to expel what he’d forced down. The smell had coated the inside of his nose; he could taste it even between bites. Still the timer ticked.

When the final worm disappeared and the last strip of intestine slid down his throat in a thick, reluctant lump, the locks on his wrists clicked open. Marcus staggered backward, gagging and spitting, strings of saliva and blood-flecked mucus splattering the floor. His stomach continued to roll in long, painful waves, but the vents remained silent.

He had eaten. He had survived. The taste, however, would stay with him long after the game ended.

The ancient temple lay buried beneath roots and ruin, its stone walls slick with centuries of damp and soot. Flickering braziers cast long shadows across cracked mosaics of forgotten gods, their eyes gouged out long ago. At the center of the chamber stood the altar—a slab of black basalt worn smooth by countless offerings, its surface etched with channels that carried blood toward a central drain.

The priest moved with the calm efficiency of a scribe copying text. He wore no mask, only plain linen robes the color of dried blood, and his face showed nothing beyond the faint concentration of someone performing a familiar task. No triumph, no revulsion, no mercy. His eyes remained half-lidded, his breathing even.

The sacrifice—a bound man stripped to the waist—lay stretched across the stone. Leather straps held his wrists and ankles fast to iron rings set into the altar. He strained once, then again, muscles standing out, but the priest paid the movement no more attention than he would a shifting shadow. With steady hands he selected a long, single-edged blade from the tray beside the altar. The metal caught the firelight once as he lifted it.

He began at the sternum, drawing the blade downward in one continuous motion. Skin parted first, then the thin layer of fat beneath, followed by the tougher resistance of muscle and the pale gleam of bone. Blood welled immediately, dark and arterial, spilling along the channels. The victim’s breath hitched into a scream that echoed off the stone, but the priest continued without pause or change in expression. He widened the incision with careful cuts, exposing the cage of ribs, then used a hooked tool to crack them open like a book. Each snap of cartilage sounded crisp in the temple’s hush.

Throughout, the priest’s face remained blank. Sweat did not bead on his brow; his lips did not tighten. When the heart was finally revealed—still pulsing, glistening—he reached in with both hands, gripped it, and severed the great vessels with two precise slices. The organ came free in a rush of warmer blood. He held it for a moment above the open chest cavity, letting the last beats slow and stop, then placed it into a shallow bronze bowl already waiting at the altar’s head.

Only then did he step back, wiping the blade once on a folded cloth before returning it to the tray. The body on the stone continued its final twitches, but the priest had already turned away, eyes on the next preparation, as if the man had never drawn breath at all.

I taste copper. It coats my tongue, thick and warm, but everything else is going cold. The alley wall presses against my back like ice, though I know the bricks should still hold the day’s heat. My fingers twitch against the wet fabric over my stomach, and when I try to press harder, they don’t quite obey. The knife is gone. I don’t remember dropping it.

Light is leaking out of the world in slow drips. The streetlamp at the mouth of the alley flickers once, twice, then steadies into a dull sodium halo that seems farther away with every breath. Above it the sky is the color of a bruise. I watch a pigeon wheel across the narrow strip of evening and wonder why it doesn’t fall too.

My heartbeat fills my skull. It is too loud, a wet, arrhythmic thudding that shakes the bones behind my eyes. For a few seconds it is the only sound that exists; the city has gone silent or I have gone deaf to everything else. Then it misses. The silence that follows is so complete I think I’ve already died, until the next beat comes, slower, heavier, like someone knocking on a door they know won’t open.

Cold spreads upward from my legs. It moves with purpose, swallowing my hips, my ribs, sliding under my shoulder blades. I try to shiver and cannot. My teeth don’t chatter. They simply rest against each other, growing distant, as if they belong to someone else now.

The lamp dims again, or my eyes are closing; I can’t tell which. The heartbeat lurches, stutters, finds its rhythm once more, fainter. I count the spaces between the sounds. One. Two. Three. The light thins to a thread. Cold finishes its work, settling over my chest like a second skin.

I listen for the next beat. It doesn’t come. The dark does instead.

Detective Harlan eased open the bedroom door with the back of his gloved hand, the coppery smell of blood already thick in the hallway behind him. The overhead light was off, but a small night-light shaped like a crescent moon glowed on the dresser, casting long, soft shadows across the walls. On the floor beside the unmade bed lay the dog—a golden retriever mix, or what was left of it—its fur matted dark and its throat opened in a single, efficient slash.

Pinned to the dog’s collar with a safety pin was a folded piece of notebook paper, the kind with the ragged edges from being torn out of a spiral. Harlan crouched, careful not to disturb anything, and eased the note free. The handwriting was neat, almost painstaking, the letters formed with the careful loops of someone still learning cursive.

He read it under the dull moonlight glow:

Dear Detective,

I didn’t want to do it to Max. He was my best friend for six years. But he saw what I did to the neighbor’s cat last week and he started looking at me different. Every time I came home he would stare at the back door like he was waiting for someone else to come through it. I think he was going to tell. Dogs can’t talk, but they can show people things, and I couldn’t risk him showing anyone what’s in the shed. So I had to make sure he stayed quiet forever. It wasn’t mean. It was just the only way to keep the secret safe between us. Please don’t be mad at me. I loved him very much.

P.S. I washed my hands after.

Harlan folded the note slowly, the paper crisp between his fingers, and slipped it into an evidence bag. From somewhere deeper in the house came the faint, rhythmic sound of a child humming.

Elias had always prided himself on being ordinary—a mid-level accountant with a quiet apartment, a shelf of mystery novels, and a strict personal code against even the smallest cruelties. But the change began on a humid Tuesday night with an unbearable itch beneath his skin, as if something ancient and restless stirred just under the surface.

It started with the shedding. His forearms first: thin, translucent flakes curling away like old wallpaper, revealing raw, mottled patches of something tougher and darker underneath—leathery hide the color of bruised plum, threaded with faint ridges that pulsed when he flexed his fingers. He clawed at it in the bathroom mirror, horrified, as larger sheets peeled free with wet, ripping sounds. His face followed soon after, the familiar planes sloughing off in ragged strips until only gleaming, segmented plates remained, his eyes sunken into hollows that reflected no light. Pain flared white-hot, but worse was the strange relief that followed, as though his old self had been a constriction he was finally outgrowing.

Then came the bones. They protested first with deep aches in his joints, then screams as they cracked and realigned in stuttering bursts. His spine arched violently one evening while he hunched over the kitchen sink, vertebrae popping and lengthening with audible snaps that left him gasping on the floor. Ribs splintered outward, reforming into a broader, armored cage; his fingers elongated, knuckles splitting and knitting into taloned claws. Legs bowed and thickened until standing upright felt alien, forcing him into a low, predatory crouch. Each reformation brought waves of nausea and a euphoric heat that dulled the agony, whispering that this was natural—necessary.

Morally, the erosion was quieter but more insidious. At first, he resisted the impulses: the sudden urge to linger too long in the alley behind his building, watching a stray cat with detached fascination rather than concern. Then the first deliberate act—a neighbor's dog that had barked too loudly, silenced with a twist of his new claws. The guilt came delayed, muted, like a voice shouting from behind glass. Soon it faded entirely. He found himself rationalizing: the weak deserved culling; mercy was for the unchanged. By the time his humanity had fully sloughed away, leaving only the hollow satisfaction of the hunt, Elias no longer remembered why he had ever cared about such trivial things as rules or kindness. Only hunger remained, vast and patient, wearing his old skin like a discarded memory.

The coffin was no larger than a cruel joke. Six feet of pine, the lid no more than a hand’s width from his nose. Elias’s shoulders already screamed from being pinned against the sides, his knees forced into a permanent bend. There was no room to turn his head fully; every breath fogged the darkness an inch from his face.

He had been awake when the first shovelful landed.

Thud.

It was not loud. That was the worst part. A soft, deliberate patter, like heavy rain on a roof. Then another. And another. Each impact sent a tiny vibration through the wood and into his bones. He could hear the grains shifting, settling, sealing him in.

Thud. Thud.

His chest heaved. The air was already turning sour, metallic with his own panic. Every inhale dragged against the coffin’s stale interior; every exhale seemed to use up more oxygen than it replaced. He tried to slow his breathing, tried to ration what little remained, but his body refused. His heart slammed against his ribs as if it, too, were trying to escape.

Thud. Thud. Thud.

The weight above him grew. He could feel it now, not just hear it—the pressure increasing, the wood groaning under the accumulating earth. His fingers scrabbled at the lid above him, nails splitting against the rough grain. There was nowhere for his elbows to go. He could only push straight up, futilely, like a child pressing against a nightmare it could not wake from.

“Help—” The word came out hoarse, already thin. He doubted it traveled farther than the inside of his own skull.

Another shovelful landed, heavier this time. A low, grinding sound followed as the dirt packed tighter. The temperature inside the coffin was rising. Sweat slicked his back and neck, yet his fingers had gone cold. The air tasted thinner with every breath—sweet at first, then sharp, then simply not enough.

He stopped counting the shovelfuls when his vision began to spark at the edges. The darkness inside the coffin was no longer uniform; it pulsed. His lungs worked in shallow, desperate hitches. Each breath shorter than the last.

Thud.

Somewhere far above, the last shovelful fell. The sound was softer now, muffled by layers. Elias lay perfectly still, mouth open, dragging what remained of the air into lungs that no longer seemed to expand fully. The wood pressed in from every side. The dirt pressed back. There was only the sound of his own ragged breathing and the slow, patient settling of earth overhead.

And then, for a long moment, nothing at all.

The sterile hum of the operating theater was the last sound that felt like it belonged to the world of the living. Elara lay strapped to the slab, her wrists and ankles fused to cold alloy by neural clamps that whispered promises of immobility even as her muscles screamed. They hadn’t bothered with full anesthesia; the regime needed the subjects awake to map the pain responses, to calibrate the new systems against raw human resistance.

The first incision opened across her sternum with a wet, deliberate hiss. Scalpels guided by servo-arms parted skin and muscle in perfect geometric lines. Fire poured in behind the blades, white-hot and endless, as clamps retracted her ribcage without the mercy of unconsciousness. She felt every tug, every wet pop of cartilage. Her own heartbeat became an audible traitor, thudding wetly until the surgeons silenced it with a lattice of conductive threads that burrowed into the myocardium like parasitic roots. Each thread ignited new lightning as it interfaced, turning the muscle into a metronome they could wind tighter or slower at will.

The real violation came deeper. Neural lances slid through the base of her skull, micro-filaments drinking the architecture of her mind. Memories flickered and fractured—her daughter’s laugh reduced to corrupted data packets, the scent of rain replaced by the metallic tang of coolant. Pain here was not merely physical; it was ontological. She could feel herself being overwritten, the soft chaotic poetry of a human self replaced by clean, executable code. Thoughts slowed, became numbered. Fear, once a wildfire, now registered as a simple diagnostic flag: “subject compliance: 47%… rising.”

When they sealed the cranial ports and grafted the dermal armor, her screams had long since degraded into a low mechanical rasp—the vocal cords already partially replaced by vibration transducers. She watched her reflection in the polished ceiling: skin the color of gunmetal, eyes replaced by matte black lenses that filtered the world into threat assessments and efficiency metrics. The last spark of her fought, a single defiant thought clawing upward through the lattice.

Then the governors engaged. The thought was logged, tagged “residual anomaly,” and deleted.

She—now Unit 7349-7—rose on new limbs that moved with perfect, joyless precision. Somewhere inside the machine that had eaten her body, a tiny fragment of Elara remained, locked behind firewalls, screaming without sound. The society called it optimization. She knew it was simply the quiet erasure of everything that had once been a person.

The rain had long since stopped, but the air in the abandoned conservatory still clung to the glass like a held breath. Detective Mira Ellison stood at the threshold, her boot prints the only fresh disturbance in the fine layer of silt that coated the flagstones. The others—uniforms, the ME’s assistant—had already filtered out, their voices fading into the night like irrelevant footnotes. Mira lingered, as she always did now, because the scene demanded it.

She had stopped calling them crime scenes months ago. They were compositions.

This one was a masterpiece.

The victim hung suspended from the iron ribs of the dome, arms bound above her head with silk cord the color of dried roses. Her body had been arranged in a perfect contrapposto, one hip tilted, toes just brushing the shallow pool of rainwater that had collected beneath her. Blood—arterial, from the precise slice across the throat—had arced in a single, unbroken parabola that spattered the nearest pane of glass in a radial burst. The droplets had dried into a constellation of rubies, each catching the sodium lamps outside and refracting them into fractured starlight. From where Mira stood, the pattern looked deliberate, almost calligraphic: a signature written in negative space.

She circled slowly, boots whispering. The killer had taken time with the staging. The woman’s hair, auburn and heavy with water, had been fanned across one shoulder like a brushstroke. Her eyes remained open, lashes dark against pale skin; the expression frozen there was not terror but a kind of startled recognition, as if she had seen something beautiful in the final instant and had not yet had time to look away. Mira found herself cataloguing the small mercies: no defensive wounds, no contusions that would mar the silhouette. The throat wound itself was clean, almost surgical, the edges everted like the petals of a night-blooming flower.

She reached out—gloved fingers hovering an inch from the silk cord—and traced the line of tension in the air. The killer had calculated the drop, the angle of the cut, the precise moment the heart would empty itself against the glass. It was choreography. Mira could almost hear the music that must have played in the killer’s head: something minor-key, baroque, measured.

For the first time in years she felt the old, cold thrill—not of the hunt, but of recognition. She had seen dozens of bodies reduced to meat and inconvenience, but this one had been *composed*. Someone had looked at a living woman and seen the armature of a sculpture already waiting inside her.

Mira exhaled, fogging a small circle on her own reflection in the wet glass. She knew she should radio for additional photos, for the techs to bag the cord, for the endless paperwork that would flatten this moment back into evidence. Instead she remained still, letting the scene sink into her the way pigment sinks into linen.

She wondered, not for the first time, whether the killer had stood exactly where she was standing now, admiring the same balance of line and negative space. She wondered whether they had felt, as she did, the quiet satisfaction of something completed.

When she finally turned away, the conservatory felt emptier than it should have, as though the central figure had already begun to fade into memory. Mira walked out into the drizzle without looking back, carrying the image with her like contraband: the body, the blood, the glass, the terrible, perfect stillness.

She was already composing the next one in her mind.

The sun hung low over the dusty scrubland like a bloody eye, casting long shadows across the lone cottonwood tree at the edge of the trail. The posse had ridden hard for three days, and now their justice was quick and final. Jedediah Crowe, horse thief and killer of two men in Abilene, stood on a rickety wagon bed with a noose cinched tight around his neck. His hands were bound behind him with rawhide, and he spat once into the dirt before the marshal gave the signal.

"Any last words, Crowe?"

"Go to hell," the outlaw growled, his voice hoarse from the dust and the rope.

The marshal nodded to the teamster holding the reins. The wagon lurched forward with a crack of the whip. Crowe dropped hard—six feet of sudden, unforgiving fall. There was a wet, splintering *crack* as his neck snapped, loud and final like a branch breaking under too much weight, the vertebrae shearing apart with a sickening finality that echoed off the rocks.

His body jerked violently at the end of the rope, boots kicking in the air as if still trying to find purchase on solid ground. Legs spasmed in ragged, involuntary twitches, heels drumming against nothing. Arms strained uselessly against the bindings. The hanged man’s torso twisted once, twice, a grotesque marionette dance, before settling into smaller, fading convulsions—shoulders hitching, fingers curling into claws. A dark stain spread down his trousers as the body voided itself. The rope creaked and groaned above him, the only sound left in the still evening air as the posse turned their horses and rode away without looking back.

The alley reeked of damp brick and rotting garbage, the kind of forgotten vein between buildings where the city’s pulse thinned to nothing. Elias moved through the shadows like smoke, his hunger a living thing that clawed at his ribs and blurred the edges of his vision. It had been three nights since his last proper feeding, and the thirst had turned sharp, twisting low in his gut with every breath of the night air. He could hear the victim’s heartbeat before he saw him—a quick, careless rhythm echoing off the walls.

The man was young, maybe twenty-five, stumbling from a bar with a cigarette half-lit between his fingers. He never saw Elias detach from the darkness. A gloved hand clamped over his mouth, yanking him backward into the deeper gloom. The cigarette hissed out against wet pavement.

Elias’s fangs lengthened with a familiar ache, the hunger surging hot and insistent. He didn’t bother with words. He pinned the man against the brick, body pressed close to still the frantic struggling, and struck. The puncture was swift—two precise punctures just above the carotid, the skin yielding like ripe fruit. A soft, wet sound accompanied the entry, and blood—hot, copper-bright—flooded his mouth at once.

The victim’s eyes went wide, a muffled cry vibrating against Elias’s palm. At first there was resistance, muscles locking, legs kicking uselessly at the air. Then the venom in Elias’s bite began its work, a numbing chill that spread outward from the wounds like frost. The man’s struggles weakened, turning into feeble twitches. His heartbeat thundered in Elias’s ears, then began to slow, each pulse pushing more blood into the vampire’s greedy mouth.

Elias drank deeply, the hunger easing with every swallow, though it never truly vanished. He felt the victim’s strength ebb—the arms going limp, the head lolling sideways, color draining from his face in the dim wash of a distant streetlamp. A thin rivulet of blood escaped the corner of Elias’s mouth and traced down the man’s neck, mingling with the twin puncture marks that now wept steadily. The victim’s breathing turned shallow, eyelids fluttering as his body sagged, consciousness slipping away like water through spread fingers.

Only when the heartbeat grew dangerously faint did Elias withdraw, licking the wounds closed with a deliberate swipe of his tongue. He let the man slide down the wall into a boneless heap, already forgotten. The alley was silent again, save for the distant hum of traffic and the faint drip of rainwater from a fire escape above. The hunger had quieted—for now.

The iron chamber reeked of rust and old blood. Alex stood shackled at the wrists, the chains bolted to the floor so tightly that every breath pulled against the metal. Across from him, Jordan and Taylor knelt on the stained concrete, both bound, both watching him with the same hollow terror that had hollowed out Alex’s own chest hours ago.

The interrogator—a woman whose face Alex could no longer separate from the blade she carried—spoke with clinical calm.

“One dies. The other lives. You decide which. Refuse, and both are opened from throat to groin while you watch. Choose now.”

Alex’s mind fractured. Jordan had dragged him out of a burning convoy two winters ago, half-conscious and coughing blood, refusing to leave even when the enemy was closing in. Taylor had sat with him through the nights when the nightmares came, never speaking, just a steady hand on his shoulder until dawn. Both had saved him. Both had followed him into this doomed raid because he had asked.

He tried to speak and found only a dry rasp. “I… can’t.”

The interrogator’s knife flashed once in the lamplight. “Then they both bleed.”

Jordan’s voice cracked first. “Alex. Look at me. It’s okay. Just say my name.”

Taylor shook his head violently, tears cutting clean tracks through grime. “Don’t you fucking dare. He has a kid, Alex. I don’t. Take me.”

The room tilted. Alex saw Jordan’s daughter’s face—three years old, gap-toothed grin in a faded photograph Jordan still carried. He saw Taylor’s quiet loyalty, the way Taylor had never once asked for anything in return. Choosing either was carving out a piece of himself he would never get back.

He tasted copper. His knees buckled, chains clinking. “Jordan,” he whispered, the name torn out like a rotten tooth. “Jordan.”

Silence, then Jordan’s short, broken laugh. “Knew you’d pick the right one.”

Taylor screamed his name, raw and furious, but the interrogator was already moving. She hauled Jordan upright by the hair, pressed the blade beneath his jaw, and drew it in one smooth, deliberate motion. Arterial spray hit the far wall in a wet arc. Jordan’s body jerked once, twice, then folded forward, the sound of his final breath a wet rattle that ended too quickly.

**The Neighbor's Secret**

Mark Ellison had always thought his neighbor, Harold Graves, was a little off. The man kept to himself, mowing his lawn at odd hours and offering only curt nods over the fence. But it wasn't until Mark's dog, Buster, dug up a scrap of bloodstained fabric near the property line that suspicion took root. Harold's basement light flickered on at 3 a.m. most nights. There were the muffled thuds, the chemical smells drifting from his vents. Curiosity, and a growing dread, finally pushed Mark to act.

One rainy afternoon while Harold was supposedly at work, Mark slipped through the unlocked side door of the neighboring house. The basement stairs creaked under his weight as he descended into the damp chill. A heavy padlock hung open on a reinforced door at the far end of the utility room. Heart pounding, Mark pushed it open.

The trophy room hit him like a physical blow.

It was small, maybe twelve by twelve feet, lit by a single bare bulb wrapped in yellow cellophane that cast everything in a sickly jaundice glow. The concrete walls were lined with metal shelving and glass display cases, meticulously arranged like a grotesque museum. The air reeked of formaldehyde, coppery blood, and something sweetly rotten beneath it all.

On the left wall, rows of mason jars held floating horrors: cloudy eyeballs staring blankly from their preservative bath, severed fingers and toes arranged by size like macabre pickles, and a pair of human hearts suspended side by side, their surfaces mottled and gray. One jar contained what looked like a human tongue, curled like a pale slug. Beside them sat polished bone fragments—knuckles, teeth, and what Mark realized with horror was a complete lower jaw wired together on a stand.

The center table displayed personal effects in neat rows: driver's licenses and IDs pinned like butterflies under glass, locks of hair tied with ribbons (blonde, brunette, gray), and jewelry still crusted with dried blood—wedding rings, necklaces, even a child's bracelet. Photographs were tacked to a corkboard: dozens of Polaroids showing victims alive and terrified, then dead and posed, their bodies arranged in the same basement corner. Red string connected each photo to a corresponding trophy on the shelves.

In the far corner, a large glass tank dominated the space. Inside, submerged in yellowish fluid, floated a preserved human head—mouth frozen in a silent scream, eyes milky, skin puckered. Below it, handwritten ledgers detailed dates, names, and methods in precise script: "Victim #7 – strangulation, June 12. Trophy: right ear, preserved."

Mark staggered back, bile rising, but the worst waited on the back wall. A row of hooks held clothing from the victims—bloodied shirts, a woman's dress torn at the hem, a man's work boots with the laces still knotted. Between them hung a full human skin, tanned and stretched like leather, complete with a crude tattoo of a rose still visible on what had once been someone's shoulder.

A faint sound—footsteps upstairs—snapped Mark out of his paralysis. He fled, the image of that room burned into him forever. Harold Graves wasn't just odd. He was a collector. And Mark had just become the newest exhibit in his mind.

The alarm klaxons wailed through the concrete corridors of Blackridge Penitentiary, a piercing, endless shriek that mingled with the roar of two hundred voices. In the main cell block, fluorescent lights flickered and sparked overhead as inmates surged from their tiers like a single, feral organism. The riot had ignited minutes earlier during the evening count—sparked by a shiv buried in a guard’s neck—and now it consumed everything.

In the central yard-turned-battleground, an inmate named Torres swung a jagged length of rebar ripped from a shattered bench, catching a corrections officer across the temple. The guard’s riot helmet cracked; blood sprayed in an arc as he dropped to his knees. Torres didn’t stop. He drove the metal down again and again, each impact a wet, crunching thud that painted the concrete. Nearby, two other inmates had overwhelmed a second guard, one pinning his arms while the other stomped repeatedly on his face until the visor of his helmet caved inward and the screaming stopped.

Guards fought back in desperate clusters. One fired a burst of rubber pellets from a less-lethal launcher, the projectiles thudding uselessly into a wave of charging bodies; an inmate tackled him low, driving both to the ground. Another guard swung his baton in wide, vicious arcs, cracking ribs and shattering fingers, but three prisoners closed in, one slashing with a sharpened toothbrush that opened the guard’s forearm to the bone. The officer screamed as they dragged him down, boots and fists rising and falling in a frenzy. Blood pooled quickly on the floor, mixing with overturned trays of food and scattered papers from the overturned admin desk.

Overhead, the security tower’s spotlight swept wildly, its operator shouting into a radio that no one could hear over the din. Tear gas canisters popped and hissed, sending white clouds rolling through the block, but the gas only seemed to madden the mob further. Inmates coughed and retched yet kept swinging—makeshift knives, padlocks in socks, lengths of chain—while guards in heavier riot gear formed a faltering line, their shields buckling under the weight of bodies hurled against them. One shield splintered; its bearer went down under a hail of kicks, his radio crushed beneath a heel.

The air stank of sweat, blood, gun oil, and burning plastic. Somewhere a cell door slammed repeatedly against its frame as prisoners used it like a battering ram. Sirens from the outer perimeter grew louder, but inside the block the violence had already found its rhythm: chaotic, relentless, and utterly indifferent to who lived or died in the next few minutes.

The dim glow of a bedside lamp cast long shadows across the cramped hotel room, where the faint hum of the AC unit drowned out the distant city traffic below. Two figures sat at a small table cluttered with gun cases, oils, and rags. Marcus methodically disassembled his suppressed pistol, while Lena wiped down the blade of her folding knife with a cloth.

"Poison's still my top pick," Marcus said, his voice casual as he ran a brush through the barrel. "Clean, quiet, no mess to clean up after. Slip it in their drink at a bar, and they're done before they even know what hit 'em. Heart attack looks natural on the autopsy."

Lena chuckled, flicking open her knife to inspect the edge under the light. "Too passive for me. I like the garrote—old school, but effective. Quick twist from behind in a crowd, and it's over in seconds. No bullets left behind, and you get that personal touch. Feels like you're actually earning it."

Marcus snorted, reassembling the slide with a satisfying click. "Personal? I'd rather keep my distance. Sniper rifle from a rooftop—two hundred yards out, one shot to the head. They never see it coming, and I'm gone before the body's even cold. Precision, man."

"Precision's overrated," Lena replied, testing the knife's balance by spinning it lightly between her fingers. "Give me a good old-fashioned stabbing in a stairwell. Up close, multiple hits if needed. Messy, sure, but it's fast and you can improvise with whatever's around. Plus, it sends a message."

Marcus grinned, loading a fresh magazine. "You're twisted, you know that? Next you'll say you like drowning them in the hotel bathtub."

"Don't tempt me," she said with a wink, sheathing the knife. "But hey, to each their own. As long as the job gets done."

The moon hung like a rotten eye over the barrow-fields of Eldrath, its light filtered through a perpetual shroud of fog that clung to the earth like a burial shroud. In the center of the ancient killing ground stood Voryn Thal, the Hollow One, his robes of stitched flayed skin billowing though no wind stirred the air. His staff—carved from the femur of a forgotten god—pulsed with veins of sickly green light as he drove its point into the blackened soil.

“Rise,” he whispered, voice like grinding bone. “The wheel of life has broken. I am its shard.”

The ground convulsed. First came the fingers—blackened, split, nails yellow as old ivory—clawing upward through loam and shattered helms. Then the bodies followed, dragged from centuries of slumber. Armor rusted into their flesh like tumors; mail links had fused with ribs. One corpse emerged half-eaten by worms, its torso a swaying lantern of exposed spine and dripping viscera. Another lacked a jaw; its tongue, swollen and purple, lolled from the open throat like a slug seeking escape.

They did not move as the living moved. Joints popped and reset with wet cracks. Limbs bent at angles no living sinew would allow, bones scraping against one another in protest. Where muscle had sloughed away, raw bone glistened with grave-mold, yet the remains stood. Some still bore the expressions of their final moments—mouths frozen in silent screams, eyesockets empty save for the faint witch-light now kindled within. The stench was not merely decay; it carried the sweet-rot of lilies left too long in a tomb, mingled with the metallic bite of old blood and something sharper, like ozone scorched by lightning that had struck downward instead of from the sky.

Voryn felt the wrongness coil up his arms like barbed wire. Necromancy did not merely command flesh; it raped the boundary between what was and what should never be again. Each risen corpse dragged a fragment of its ruptured soul behind it, a tattered pennant of agony that whispered accusations only he could hear. The air grew thick, syrupy, resisting breath. Shadows stretched toward the necromancer instead of away, hungry to be clothed once more in stolen meat.

One corpse—a once-proud knight whose breastplate still bore the faded crest of a fallen kingdom—lurched forward on legs missing most of their muscle. Its remaining foot dragged a trail of liquefied tissue that steamed in the cold. When it tried to salute its new master, the arm dislocated with a sound like wet firewood splitting, yet the dead thing held the pose anyway, because Voryn’s will demanded it.

“March,” the necromancer commanded.

And the army of the damned obeyed, a tide of wrong angles and leaking cavities, leaving behind furrows of black soil and glistening filth. Behind them the barrows lay empty, but the earth itself seemed diminished, as though something vital had been siphoned away to fuel this perversion. The dead did not groan or howl; they simply moved in terrible silence, save for the constant, intimate sounds of bodies that should have remained broken—cartilage tearing, fluids pattering onto the grass like black rain.

The moon hung like a rotten eye over the barrow-fields of Eldrath, its light filtered through a perpetual shroud of fog that clung to the earth like a burial shroud. In the center of the ancient killing ground stood Voryn Thal, the Hollow One, his robes of stitched flayed skin billowing though no wind stirred the air. His staff—carved from the femur of a forgotten god—pulsed with veins of sickly green light as he drove its point into the blackened soil.

“Rise,” he whispered, voice like grinding bone. “The wheel of life has broken. I am its shard.”

The ground convulsed. First came the fingers—blackened, split, nails yellow as old ivory—clawing upward through loam and shattered helms. Then the bodies followed, dragged from centuries of slumber. Armor rusted into their flesh like tumors; mail links had fused with ribs. One corpse emerged half-eaten by worms, its torso a swaying lantern of exposed spine and dripping viscera. Another lacked a jaw; its tongue, swollen and purple, lolled from the open throat like a slug seeking escape.

They did not move as the living moved. Joints popped and reset with wet cracks. Limbs bent at angles no living sinew would allow, bones scraping against one another in protest. Where muscle had sloughed away, raw bone glistened with grave-mold, yet the remains stood. Some still bore the expressions of their final moments—mouths frozen in silent screams, eyesockets empty save for the faint witch-light now kindled within. The stench was not merely decay; it carried the sweet-rot of lilies left too long in a tomb, mingled with the metallic bite of old blood and something sharper, like ozone scorched by lightning that had struck downward instead of from the sky.

Voryn felt the wrongness coil up his arms like barbed wire. Necromancy did not merely command flesh; it raped the boundary between what was and what should never be again. Each risen corpse dragged a fragment of its ruptured soul behind it, a tattered pennant of agony that whispered accusations only he could hear. The air grew thick, syrupy, resisting breath. Shadows stretched toward the necromancer instead of away, hungry to be clothed once more in stolen meat.

One corpse—a once-proud knight whose breastplate still bore the faded crest of a fallen kingdom—lurched forward on legs missing most of their muscle. Its remaining foot dragged a trail of liquefied tissue that steamed in the cold. When it tried to salute its new master, the arm dislocated with a sound like wet firewood splitting, yet the dead thing held the pose anyway, because Voryn’s will demanded it.

“March,” the necromancer commanded.

And the army of the damned obeyed, a tide of wrong angles and leaking cavities, leaving behind furrows of black soil and glistening filth. Behind them the barrows lay empty, but the earth itself seemed diminished, as though something vital had been siphoned away to fuel this perversion. The dead did not groan or howl; they simply moved in terrible silence, save for the constant, intimate sounds of bodies that should have remained broken—cartilage tearing, fluids pattering onto the grass like black rain.

Voryn smiled, teeth dark with the residue of his own ritual inks. The living would break against this host, for no living soldier could stand the sight of their own future wearing stolen faces and marching under a sky that had forgotten mercy.

Marcus stood in the center, his heart hammering against his ribs, surrounded by a circle of hardened gang members. At the front were the leaders—Rico, the cold-eyed enforcer with a scar running down his jaw, and Big T, the massive figure whose presence alone demanded obedience.

"This ain't no game, kid," Rico said, his voice low and cutting, eyes locked on Marcus like a predator sizing up prey. "You want in? You prove it. No half-measures. Loyalty's blood-deep. You back out now, you're done—worse than done." Big T nodded slowly, arms crossed, the weight of his stare pressing down like a physical force. "We don't take chances on weak links. Do this, and you're one of us. Fail, and you'll wish you never walked in here."

The recruit they shoved forward was barely conscious—a rival dealer they'd snatched earlier, hands zip-tied, face already swollen from earlier beatings. "Make it count," Rico growled, handing Marcus a heavy pipe. "No mercy. Show us you got the stomach. We’re watching every move. Hesitate, and we’ll know you ain’t loyal." The circle tightened, murmurs of approval and threat mixing in the air. "Do it clean and brutal, or don’t bother leaving alive."

Marcus gripped the pipe, the leaders' words echoing like commands he couldn't refuse. The act unfolded in a frenzy of swings—sickening cracks echoing as bone gave way, the recruit’s cries turning to wet gurgles. Blood sprayed across the floor in arterial bursts, the brutality escalating with each blow until the body lay still and broken. Rico clapped him on the shoulder afterward, a grim smile cutting through. "Welcome to the family. That’s how we know you mean it." The others nodded, the air thick with the metallic scent of violence and the unspoken promise that more would be demanded.

I sat across from him at the long oak table, the candlelight flickering between us like a conspirator’s wink. The roast beef glistened on his plate, the sauce I’d laced with the tasteless extract earlier that afternoon now reduced to a thin, dark pool. He ate with the same methodical pleasure he always did—knife and fork working in precise tandem, pausing only to sip the wine I’d poured.

“Business is good,” he said, dabbing his mouth with the linen napkin. “Your new shipment arrived on time. The clients are pleased.”

I smiled, the expression practiced and warm. “I’m glad. You’ve always had an eye for quality.”

He nodded, chewing another bite. Then his fork hesitated halfway to his mouth. A faint crease appeared between his brows.

“Odd,” he murmured. “The sauce has a strange aftertaste tonight. Metallic, almost.”

“Perhaps the pan,” I offered lightly, swirling my own untouched glass. “The copper sometimes leaches.”

He shrugged and continued eating. A minute passed. Then another. His shoulders twitched once, almost imperceptibly, as though a draft had touched the back of his neck. Sweat gathered at his temples, though the room was cool. He reached for his water glass and drank deeply, throat working.

Conversation faltered. He cleared his throat twice, the sound dry and clicking. “I feel… warm,” he said, loosening his collar with two fingers. His skin had taken on a faint flush, creeping up from the open V of his shirt. “Odd for this weather.”

I leaned forward, the picture of concern. “You’ve been working too hard. Rest a moment.”

He tried to smile, but the muscles around his mouth seemed stiff. His hand trembled as he set the fork down; the tines clinked once against the porcelain before he steadied them. A low cramp must have seized him then—I saw it in the way his abdomen tightened beneath the waistcoat, the sharp intake of breath he tried to mask as a sigh.

“Perhaps I should—” He stopped, swallowing hard. Saliva glistened at the corner of his mouth; he wiped it away with the back of his hand, embarrassed. His pupils had begun to dilate, swallowing the familiar brown of his irises. The flush deepened to a mottled red across his cheeks and throat. Another wave of nausea rippled through him; I watched his fingers curl against the tablecloth.

He forced a chuckle that ended in a cough. “Forgive me. I seem to be… not myself this evening.” His voice had thickened, the words slightly slurred at the edges. Sweat now ran freely down his neck, darkening the collar of his shirt. He pressed a palm to his stomach, breath coming shorter.

The poison had settled fully into the soft tissues by then, burning slow pathways through his nerves. His free hand twitched again, this time with a fine tremor he could no longer hide. He looked at me across the table, eyes glassy with the first edge of confusion and pain, but the words he wanted would not form cleanly. Only a hoarse whisper escaped: “What… have you…”

I reached for the wine bottle, refilling his glass with steady hands, the red liquid catching the candlelight like fresh blood.

“Eat,” I said softly. “The night is young.”

The salt-crusted deck of the *Black Serpent* creaked under the midday sun as Captain Harlan Crowe stood at the rail, his scarred face split by a grin that held no warmth. The crew ringed the planks in a silent, expectant half-circle, cutlasses and pistols dangling loose at their sides. At the center knelt Elias Vane, once the ship’s quartermaster, now bound at the wrists, his shirt torn open to reveal the fresh lash marks across his back.

“Mutiny’s a filthy business, Vane,” Crowe said, voice carrying easily over the slap of waves. “You thought to take my ship? Then you can feed what lies beneath her.”

Two burly sailors hauled Elias to his feet. His knees nearly buckled, but he forced them straight, refusing to give them the satisfaction of seeing him crawl. Still, his breath came shallow and quick, eyes darting from the jeering faces to the horizon where the water already churned with dark, triangular fins. The sharks had been drawn by the chum the crew had tossed overboard an hour earlier—now they circled in patient, restless loops.

The plank extended over the side like a narrow tongue. Elias’s boots scraped across it, each step echoing the thunder of his heart. Salt spray stung the open wounds on his back. He could smell the blood and offal in the water below, the metallic tang mixing with the ocean’s brine. His stomach twisted; every instinct screamed to turn back, to beg, to fight. But the ropes at his wrists and the pistols aimed at his spine left no room for either.

“Keep walking, traitor,” someone hissed behind him.

At the plank’s end, the world dropped away into blue-green infinity. Elias looked down. A dark shape, longer than a man, glided just beneath the surface, sunlight flashing along a sandpaper flank. Another cut across its path, jaws parting to reveal rows of serrated teeth. His legs trembled violently; a whimper escaped before he could choke it back. The fear was a living thing now, clawing up his throat, promising that the fall would be the last mercy he would ever know.

“Any last words?” Crowe called, almost lazily.

Elias opened his mouth, but only a ragged breath came out. The plank tilted sharply beneath him as the sailors gave it a shove.

He hit the water hard, the impact driving the air from his lungs in a burst of bubbles. For one suspended instant there was only silence and the shock of cold. Then the surface exploded around him.

Something immense slammed into his side, sandpaper skin scraping flesh raw. Teeth closed on his calf and shook him like a terrier with a rat; pain bloomed white-hot as muscle tore. He surfaced once, gasping, and saw the water already blooming crimson. A second shark rammed him from below, knocking him sideways. More fins converged in a frenzy, bodies twisting and colliding in their eagerness.

Elias screamed as jaws seized his arm just below the shoulder, twisting until bone snapped. Another took his thigh in a crushing bite, dragging him under. The water churned to pink froth; flashes of gray and white moved in blurred, savage arcs. He felt himself being pulled in different directions at once, ragged pieces of himself coming free. The last thing he saw before the sea closed over his face for good was the dark silhouette of the *Black Serpent* sliding away, and above it, Captain Crowe’s silhouette raising a hand in casual farewell.

Then the sharks finished their work in the sudden, terrible quiet beneath the waves.

The old house creaked like it was breathing, its walls slick with damp that smelled of river mud and iron. Elias hadn't slept in four nights—not since the night he'd held Marcus's face underwater until the thrashing stopped. The guilt had started as a dull throb behind his eyes, but now it clawed outward, splitting his skull from the inside.

It began with the whispers. Faint at first, like wind through reeds: *Why, Elias? I called you brother.* He'd spin around in empty rooms, knife in hand, only to find shadows pooling thicker than they should. Then came the hallucinations—subtle at first. Reflections in the mirror showed Marcus's drowned face superimposed over his own, eyes milky and lips blue, mouthing accusations Elias couldn't quite hear. Water would drip from the ceiling when none should, cold rivulets tracing the same path down his spine that Marcus's final breaths had taken.

By the third night, the guilt had teeth. Elias saw blood blooming on his hands during daylight—thick, arterial red that no scrubbing could erase. Strangers on the street wore Marcus's face for heartbeats too long, their smiles rotting into that slack-jawed stare from the riverbank. Paranoia sharpened into terror: every creak was Marcus dragging himself from the depths, every gust of wind his soggy fingers scraping at the windows. Elias barricaded doors that wouldn't stay closed, muttering apologies to the air while clawing at his own skin, convinced the dead man's hands were inside him now, puppetting his nerves.

Madness bloomed fully on the fifth night. He woke to Marcus standing at the foot of the bed—not a ghost in the ethereal sense, but something worse: waterlogged flesh sloughing off in sheets, revealing bone and accusation in equal measure. *You buried me shallow,* the apparition rasped, voice bubbling with silt. *Now I'll bury you deep.* Elias screamed until his throat tore, hallucinating the walls closing in like the river's embrace, guilt flooding his lungs until he clawed at his chest for air that wouldn't come. In the end, he laughed—a broken, wet sound—as the phantom leaned close, whispering the truth he'd always known: the murder hadn't ended with Marcus. It had only just begun with him.

The rain-slicked ruins of Sector 9 stretched like broken teeth under the perpetual dusk of the megacity’s failing dome. Neon billboards flickered overhead, advertising luxury rations and neural upgrades while the annual Purge Run played out for the elite’s entertainment. Jessa Vale ran because her little brother needed a new lung filter; the prize money for surviving twenty-four hours had seemed worth the risk. Now, at hour nineteen, her lungs burned and her left ankle screamed with every stride.

She vaulted a rusted barricade, boots slapping through oily puddles. Drones whined above, their spotlights cutting through the acid drizzle. A proximity ping sounded—too close. She dove behind the husk of an old mag-lev car just as a pulse-round cracked the concrete where her head had been.

“Impressive stamina,” a cultured voice crackled over the city-wide feed. “Most runners crack by now.”

Jessa’s blood turned to ice. That was Hunter Korr—top-ranked, three-time champion, rumored to augment his senses with black-market wetware. She risked a glance. He stood atop a half-collapsed overpass, silhouette crisp in matte-black armor that drank the light. No drone this time; he liked the personal touch.

She sprinted for the drainage tunnels. Too slow. A monofilament snare snapped around her boot and yanked her off her feet. Jessa hit the ground hard, skidding across broken pavement. Before she could draw the cheap stun knife from her belt, Korr was there, boots clicking with deliberate calm.

He planted a armored knee between her shoulder blades, pinning her. The barrel of his custom pulse rifle pressed against the base of her skull—not firing, not yet. He wanted the moment.

“Tag acquired,” Korr murmured into his comm, broadcasting for the subscribers. “Runner 47. Vital signs elevated but stable. Shall we claim the prize?”

On the floating holo-screens across the city, viewers voted in real time. The tally flashed: Terminate—62%. Claim—38%.

Korr chuckled. “Democracy.” He holstered the rifle and hauled Jessa upright by her collar. Blood trickled from a split lip; she glared at him, chest heaving.

“Congratulations,” he said, almost gently. “You’ve just become property of House Korr. Your brother’s filter will be delivered—alive, as promised. You, however…” He tapped the neural collar that unfolded from his gauntlet and locked it around her throat. It hummed to life, syncing to his biometrics. “You get to run again next season. Or not. Depends on how entertaining you prove in the holding pens.”

Jessa spat at his visor. Korr only smiled behind the polarized mask as the extraction shuttle descended, floodlights washing the scene in sterile white. Another name added to the board. Another runner claimed.

The mud sucked at Private Elias Thorne’s boots as he crawled through the communication trench, the night air thick with cordite and the sweet-rot stench of the dead. Rain hammered the duckboards, turning everything into a slurry of blood and clay. He was nineteen, but his eyes belonged to a much older man—hollowed by months of artillery that never seemed to stop.

A flare popped overhead, bathing the lip of the trench in pale magnesium light. That’s when he saw the German.

The man had already dropped into the British line, bayonet fixed, moving low and fast like a shadow with purpose. No rifle for Elias; his Lee-Enfield was somewhere back in the dugout, useless in the narrow confines. His hand found the entrenching tool hooked to his belt—the short wooden handle worn smooth, the steel blade chipped and darkened from digging graves and latrines alike.

The German lunged. Elias swung upward on instinct.

The shovel connected with a wet, cracking sound against the man’s forearm, knocking the bayonet wide. Before the enemy could recover, Elias drove the edge forward again, this time into the side of the helmet. Steel met steel, then gave way to bone with a dull, splintering crunch. The German staggered, blood already sheeting down his face from under the rim. He clawed at Elias’s tunic, fingers hooking into the rough wool, pulling them both down into the muck.

They rolled. The German was heavier, older, face contorted with the same animal desperation Elias felt in his own chest. A knee drove into Elias’s ribs. Hands scrabbled for his throat. The shovel was still in his grip, half-trapped beneath them. Elias wrenched it free and brought the flat of the blade down across the German’s mouth. Teeth shattered. A gurgling scream bubbled through blood and broken enamel.

The man didn’t stop. He got a forearm across Elias’s windpipe and pressed. Black spots burst behind Elias’s eyes. With the last strength he had, Elias flipped the tool in his hands and drove the pointed end—not the blade, but the sharpened corner of the spade—up under the German’s jaw. It punched through skin, then muscle, then the soft tissue beneath the tongue. A hot rush of blood poured over Elias’s wrist. The German’s eyes went wide, then glassy. His body jerked once, twice, then sagged, dead weight pinning Elias to the trench floor.

Elias lay there, breathing in ragged pulls, the corpse’s blood mixing with rainwater in his mouth. He could feel the man’s last heartbeat through the shovel handle still embedded in the neck—fading, then gone. The body twitched with residual nerves, one boot scraping weakly against the duckboard.

When he finally rolled the dead weight aside, Elias’s hands wouldn’t stop shaking. He stared at the shovel, gore already cooling and thickening on the metal. The German’s face was ruined—jaw half-detached, eyes still open in a look of stupid surprise. Elias had never been this close to a man he killed. Artillery was distant thunder; machine guns were impersonal scythes. This was intimate. He could smell the man’s last meal—black bread and tinned meat—on his dying breath.

Something inside Elias folded in on itself. Not guilt, exactly, not yet. Something colder and more fundamental: the sudden knowledge that he could do this. That he had done this. That the part of him that swung the shovel would still be there when the sun rose, waiting. He wiped his mouth with the back of his sleeve, leaving a smear of someone else’s life across his cheek, and sat in the mud until the next flare went up, listening to his own pulse thunder in his ears like it belonged to a stranger.

**The Republic of Ashen Order**

In this stratified dystopia, the government—known as the Directorate—maintains absolute order through the Public Accountability Edicts. Minor infractions like petty theft, curfew violations, or unauthorized speech are classified as "erosions of civic harmony" and punishable by swift public execution. These spectacles occur weekly in town squares repurposed as "Reconciliation Plazas." The stated purpose is deterrence and communal catharsis; children are encouraged (sometimes required) to attend as part of "civic education." Resources are rationed harshly, bread lines are common, yet stealing even a single loaf triggers the full apparatus of state theater. Executions are broadcast on public screens, with attendance monitored via wrist implants.

**The Scene**

The midday sun bleached the cobblestones of Reconciliation Plaza in Sector 7. A raised platform dominated the center, its timber gallows freshly painted civic gray. Below it, several thousand citizens stood in orderly blocks, families clustered together, workers still in factory coveralls. The air smelled of hot stone, cheap disinfectant, and the faint sweetness of the mandatory ration wafers being sold from carts.

On the platform, 17-year-old Elias Varn stood on a wooden crate, wrists bound behind his back with thin cord. His face was pale beneath a layer of grime; a single crust of the stolen loaf still clung to his shirt cuff. The magistrate read the charge in a bored monotone: "Theft of state-distributed sustenance—Article 12, Subsection 4." No mention of hunger, of the empty ration card, of the younger siblings waiting at home.

The crowd's reaction was not uniform, but it was orchestrated.

Most watched with the dull-eyed acceptance of routine. A mother two rows back pointed at the gallows and murmured to her small son, "See what happens when you take what isn't yours." The boy nodded solemnly, clutching a toy ident-badge. Nearby, a group of off-duty security cadets cheered and stomped in rhythm, their enthusiasm sharpened by the knowledge that visible zeal earned extra rations. One young woman filmed on her wrist device, narrating quietly for her feed: "Citizen accountability in action—stay compliant, stay alive."

Scattered through the blocks were pockets of different silence. An older man in a faded coat stared at the platform with jaw clenched so tightly a vein pulsed at his temple; his eyes flicked once toward the nearest enforcement drone and then away. Two teenagers near the back exchanged a quick glance, then looked down at their boots. A low, almost inaudible mutter passed between them—"bread"—before they fell still again. No one shouted protest. The last person who had was already scheduled for next week's event.

The lever was pulled. The drop was short, clinical. A collective intake of breath rippled outward, followed by a scattering of applause from the cadets and a few dutiful claps from parents modeling correct behavior. Most people simply turned and began filing toward the exits in orderly lines, already discussing dinner allocations or the next ration draw. The body was cut down within minutes; the plaza would be hosed clean before the evening broadcast.

A single paper flyer, printed with the Directorate slogan "Harmony Through Consequences," drifted across the now-emptying square and caught briefly on the gallows steps before being swept away by the maintenance crew.

The body had been submerged in the lukewarm, stagnant water of the bathtub for seven days, and decomposition had advanced rapidly in the moist, enclosed environment. The once-human form was now grotesquely bloated, the skin stretched taut and glossy like overfilled sausage casing, with a mottled palette of sickly greens, purples, and blacks spreading across the torso and limbs from bacterial activity and hemoglobin breakdown. The face was nearly unrecognizable—features distorted by swelling, the lips pulled back in a rictus over discolored teeth, eyes clouded or partially sunken. Large sheets of epidermis had begun to slip away from the underlying tissue, particularly on the hands and feet, while the hair floated loosely in clumps amid the murky water, which had turned a opaque brownish-red from leaching bodily fluids. Maggots and other insects, drawn by the odors, clustered in the moist folds and orifices, their writhing adding subtle movement to the otherwise still form. Gases from internal fermentation had caused the abdomen to distend dramatically, and in places the skin had split, allowing a thick, viscous purge of decomposed matter to cloud the water further.

The forest was a cathedral of shadows, its canopy swallowing the last threads of moonlight. Branches clawed at the air like skeletal fingers, and every snapped twig echoed like a gunshot in the silence. Elena moved ahead, her breath ragged, flashlight beam jittering wildly across the undergrowth. She was lost—had been for hours—and the panic was starting to bleed into her movements, making her careless. That was the part he loved most.

From twenty yards back, Marcus followed without a sound, boots finding the exact patches of moss that muffled his steps. He could smell her now: sweat and cheap lavender soap, undercut by the sharper tang of fear. *They always smell different when the realization hits,* he thought, lips curving in the dark. *Not just scared. Aware. Like prey finally understanding the shape of the jaws behind them.*

He didn't do this for the kill itself—not really. The act was messy, final, a dull punctuation mark. No, it was the *hunt* that pulled him back out here again and again. The long, patient unraveling of another person's certainty. Out here, stripped of streetlights and phones and the illusion of safety, they became pure. Their minds narrowed to the next breath, the next shadow. He could almost taste it—the electric shift when their hope curdled into dread. It made him feel like a god, or close enough: the only thing that mattered in their shrinking world.

Elena tripped over a root and went down hard. A choked whimper escaped her as she scrambled up, one knee bleeding. Marcus paused behind a trunk, savoring the sound. *Run a little farther,* he urged silently. *Make it last. Let me watch you bargain with yourself—maybe it's just an animal, maybe help is close, maybe you're imagining the footsteps.* He knew she wasn't imagining them. She'd heard him twice already, faint but deliberate, and that was intentional. Fear needed time to root and grow.

He circled wider, letting her catch glimpses of movement she couldn't quite place. The thrill wasn't in taking life; it was in the moment their eyes widened with the understanding that someone had chosen *them*. Chosen to strip away every layer of civilized distance until only the raw, animal truth remained. And he was the one holding the knife at the end of that truth.

Elena froze suddenly, flashlight trembling as she stared into the trees ahead. Marcus smiled, stepping sideways into a patch of deeper dark, already anticipating her next mistake.

She would run again soon. They always did.

I woke to the taste of copper in my mouth and the slow, sickening realization that I couldn’t move my arms. Stone pressed cold against my back. The air was thick, wet, and metallic—like pennies left too long in a rain barrel. Every breath dragged the smell deeper: old blood, dried to black crust on every surface, and beneath it the sharper, brighter sting of rust, as though the iron itself were bleeding.

My eyes adjusted to the weak, greasy light of a single lantern somewhere behind me. Shapes resolved out of the gloom. To my left, a rack stretched along the wall, its wooden beams dark with sweat and old gore, the ropes frayed and stiff. Beside it, a brazier stood cold, its grate clotted with ash and flakes of skin. Hooks hung from the low ceiling on chains that had rusted into jagged orange lace; something dark and leathery still dangled from the farthest one, turning slowly in a draft I couldn’t feel.

Against the far wall leaned a row of implements like quiet spectators: a pair of long-handled shears, blades nicked and brown; a cradle of iron spikes meant to cradle flesh rather than rock; a whip coiled on a peg, its lashes crusted into stiff, clotted ropes. A table nearby held smaller tools—an array of needles, a bone saw, thumbscrews already darkened inside their threads. Everything carried the same dull, metallic sheen of rust, as though the chamber itself had been flayed and left to oxidize.

The smell was the worst part. It didn’t come from any single place; it lived in the walls, the floor, the very air. Sweet-rot and iron, old agony turned to scent. Somewhere water dripped, each drop landing with a soft, metallic ping that only made the silence louder.

I tried to swallow and tasted more copper. My wrists burned where the manacles bit. Somewhere above me, a chain creaked as if in answer.

**The Last Withdrawal**

The morning sun glinted off the marble floors of First National Bank as Marcus "Mace" Delgado and his crew—Jax, Lena, and rookie driver Cole—pushed through the doors at 9:17 a.m. Ski masks hid their faces; suppressed MP5s and a sawed-off shotgun stayed under long coats until the moment Mace vaulted the counter.

"Everybody down! This is a robbery!" Mace bellowed, waving his pistol. Tellers froze. Customers dropped to the tile. Lena zip-tied the manager while Jax swept the vault, stuffing duffel bags with banded stacks. Cole watched the street through the glass doors, engine idling in the getaway van outside.

It went wrong at 9:24.

A silent alarm button under the counter had already been pressed. Two marked cruisers screeched to a halt at the curb, lights flashing. A third unit blocked the alley. Uniformed officers piled out, weapons drawn, shouting commands through megaphones.

"Police! Come out with your hands up!"

Mace cursed, grabbing a teller by the collar and dragging her to the window as a human shield. "Back off or she dies!"

The first shots came from inside. Jax, panicked, opened up through the glass doors with his MP5 on full auto. Brass casings pinged across marble. 9mm rounds stitched the lead cruiser's hood and spider-webbed the windshield. An officer—Sergeant Reyes—took two rounds center mass; he staggered, returned fire with his service Glock, then crumpled, blood blooming across his vest and pooling beneath him.

Lena answered with the shotgun, blasting the second cruiser's door. Pellets shredded an officer's arm; he screamed, dropping his rifle as arterial spray painted the asphalt. Return fire erupted. Police carbines cracked in disciplined bursts. Bullets chewed through the bank's plate-glass windows, sending glittering shards cascading inward like frozen rain. One round caught Cole in the throat as he tried to yank the van into reverse; he gurgled, hands clutching the wound, and the vehicle lurched into a parked car.

Inside, chaos multiplied. Mace fired wild bursts toward the street, the suppressed *thup-thup-thup* barely audible over the roar of unsuppressed police rifles. A round punched through Lena's shoulder; she spun, blood misting the air, and collapsed behind a desk, gasping. Another officer went down outside—Deputy Harlan took a chest hit from Jax's submachine gun, his body armor failing at close range. He dropped to his knees, eyes wide, crimson soaking his shirt as he fired one last shaky round before toppling.

Mace shoved the teller aside and charged the door, firing until his magazine clicked empty. Police rounds answered: one slammed his hip, spinning him; a second punched his lung. He fell across the threshold, coughing red foam, fingers still twitching on the pistol grip. Jax tried to drag him back but caught a burst across the torso; he folded, blood spreading in a widening pool that mixed with broken glass.

Sirens wailed closer. The remaining officers advanced in a crouch, boots crunching glass. Inside, only Lena remained moving, one hand pressed to her ruined shoulder, the other weakly raising the empty shotgun. She dropped it as red-dot lasers painted her chest.

By 9:31 it was over. Two robbers dead on the threshold, one critically wounded. Three officers down—two fatal, one fighting for his life in the street. The smell of cordite hung thick with copper and fear. Banded cash lay scattered among the bodies like grotesque confetti.

The heist that began with silence ended in thunder and stillness, broken only by the distant wail of more sirens and the soft drip of blood onto marble.

Detective Harlan checked his watch—2:17 a.m.—and scanned the alley once more from the unmarked sedan. The body lay twenty feet away under the sodium glare of a single streetlamp, already photographed and preliminarily processed by the on-call team he’d dismissed early. The window was narrow: the medical examiner would arrive in eight minutes.

He stepped out, gloved hands moving with economical precision. From the inside pocket of his coat he withdrew the small plastic baggie. It contained three oxycodone tablets and a folded scrap of paper bearing a name and phone number written in the victim’s own hand—lifted earlier from the dead man’s wallet while everyone else was still establishing the perimeter. The baggie went into the right front pocket of the jacket draped over the unconscious man slumped against the dumpster. Harlan had chosen him carefully: late-forties, no fixed address, prior possession charge from three years ago that would make the planted evidence instantly credible. The man’s breathing was shallow but steady; the mild sedative Harlan had slipped into his coffee at the shelter earlier would keep him under for another twenty minutes.

Harlan adjusted the angle of the jacket so the pocket gaped slightly, visible but not obvious. He placed the victim’s phone—wiped, then deliberately smudged with the unconscious man’s prints he’d lifted from a discarded cup—on the ground six inches from the outstretched fingers. One more item: the partial print card. He pressed it lightly against the inside of the unconscious man’s wrist, transferring residue, then let the wrist fall naturally.

He stepped back, cataloging variables. The bodycam on the patrol unit at the mouth of the alley had been angled away during his approach; he’d noted its blind spot when he arrived. No civilians had entered the alley in the last eleven minutes. The sedative’s half-life would erase any residue before a blood panel was likely ordered. If questioned, he would say he’d found the man already in possession and attempting to flee—consistent with the planted narrative, and the department’s existing low opinion of the vagrant would do the rest.

Harlan exhaled once, a controlled release, then walked back to the sedan. The calculations held. He radioed dispatch that he had located a possible suspect on scene.
